clinicalPearls: An aggressive plasma cell malignancy defined by a high proportion of circulating clonal plasma cells in the blood
May arise de novo (primary) or evolve from pre-existing multiple myeloma (secondary)
Presents with rapidly progressive symptoms including anaemia, renal impairment, hypercalcaemia and bone disease
Extramedullary involvement, such as hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, is more common than in typical myeloma
The updated definition uses a lowered threshold for circulating plasma cells compared with older criteria
It carries a worse prognosis than multiple myeloma and requires prompt, intensive treatment
High-risk cytogenetic abnormalities are frequently present
reference.pathophysiology: Plasma cell leukaemia represents a highly proliferative, often cytogenetically high-risk clone of malignant plasma cells that has lost much of its dependence on the bone marrow microenvironment, allowing widespread circulation and extramedullary spread. Monoclonal immunoglobulin production and marrow infiltration drive end-organ damage, including renal impairment from light chains, hypercalcaemia and osteolytic bone disease with cytopenias. The aggressive biology reflects the accumulation of adverse genetic lesions and explains the rapid clinical course.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple myeloma with circulating plasma cells
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film and flow cytometry quantifying circulating clonal plasma cells
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and free light chains
Bone marrow examination with cytogenetics and FISH
Renal function, calcium and markers of tumour burden
Whole-body imaging for bone and extramedullary disease
redFlags: Acute kidney injury or severe hypercalcaemia
Cord compression or pathological fracture from bone disease
Rapidly rising tumour burden with cytopenias
reference.prognosis: Plasma cell leukaemia carries a significantly worse prognosis than multiple myeloma, though outcomes have improved with modern combination therapy and, in suitable patients, stem cell transplantation; secondary disease evolving from myeloma has a particularly poor outlook.
pitfalls: Underestimating circulating plasma cells and misclassifying it as standard myeloma
Delaying intensive therapy in a rapidly progressive disease
Failing to obtain cytogenetics that guide risk assessment
management: Start prompt intensive induction combining a proteasome inhibitor (bortezomib), an immunomodulatory agent (lenalidomide) and a corticosteroid, incorporating an anti-CD38 antibody such as daratumumab
Consolidate responders with autologous stem cell transplantation, considering allogeneic transplantation in selected fit patients given the high-risk biology
Give post-transplant maintenance therapy to prolong disease control
Manage hypercalcaemia with rehydration and a bisphosphonate, and give bisphosphonate or denosumab for osteolytic bone disease
Provide supportive care with transfusion for cytopenias, tumour lysis prophylaxis, and renal protection for light-chain nephropathy
Monitor paraprotein, free light chains, renal function and marrow response, watching for early relapse
Refer urgently to haematology or haemato-oncology for combination therapy and transplant assessment
